procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated November 10, 1967 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 4 of 1967, which refused to interfere with the Single Judge's order directing prosecution of the appellant.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A Single Judge of the Patna High Court, while dismissing an appeal related to a suit filed by the appellant, directed the appellant to show cause why he should not be prosecuted under s. 199 and s. 200 of the Indian Penal Code. After the appellant showed cause, the Single Judge was not persuaded by the appellant's explanation and directed his prosecution. A Division Bench of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 4 of 1967 refused to interfere with the Single Judge's order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Jotish Chandra Chaudhary, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave challenging the order of the Division Bench of the Patna High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed the complaint against the appellant.

directions: The orders of the Division Bench and the learned Single Judge are set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the false statement in the affidavit regarding the son's date of birth was material to the object for which the declaration was made, as required for an offence under Section 199 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: In the course of a High Court appeal, the appellant was required to file an affidavit stating the dates of birth of his three minor sons to add them as parties.
The appellant, not remembering the exact dates, obtained information from his son's school and stated in the affidavit that the son's date of birth was June 9, 1954.
The son's actual date of birth was December 12, 1951.
The High Court directed that the appellant be prosecuted for making a false statement under Section 199 of the Indian Penal Code.
law: To establish an offence under Section 199 of the Indian Penal Code, it must be proven that the false statement is 'touching any point material to the object for which the declaration is made'.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the 'object' for which the affidavit was made, which was to decide on the impleadment of the minor son as a party in the pending appeal.
The Court found that the specific date of birth, whether 1954 or 1951, made no difference to the legal question of whether the son could be impleaded or whether the suit was maintainable.
It was noted that the change in the birth date did not touch upon any material point relevant to the appeal.

The Court also observed that the appellant stood to gain no advantage by providing the wrong date, and the information was obtained from school records, which weakened the case for deliberate falsehood.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision to prosecute, concluding that the false statement regarding the son's date of birth was not material to the object for which the affidavit was made. Since the incorrect date had no impact on the legal issues in the appeal (the impleadment of the son), a key ingredient of the offence under Section 199 was not satisfied.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant used the declaration containing the false statement 'corruptly', as required for an offence under Section 200 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The appellant filed an affidavit in court stating an incorrect date of birth for his son (June 9, 1954, instead of December 12, 1951).
The appellant claimed he obtained this incorrect information from school records.
The incorrect date of birth did not make any difference to the outcome of the legal proceedings in which the affidavit was used.
law: One of the essential ingredients of an offence under Section 200 of the Indian Penal Code is that the false declaration must be used or attempted to be used 'corruptly'.
application: The Court noted that it had not been explained how the declaration was used 'corruptly'.
The Court found that the appellant stood to gain no advantage by providing the wrong date of birth.
Since the false statement was immaterial to the case and provided no benefit to the appellant, the Court determined that the 'corruptly' element of the offence was not satisfied.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim that the appellant acted 'corruptly' because he gained no advantage from the false statement, and it was not material to the legal issue at hand. Therefore, a key requirement for an offence under Section 200 of the IPC was not met.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the prosecution of the appellant, considering he stood to gain no advantage from the incorrect statement and had obtained the information from school records.

facts: In a High Court appeal, the appellant filed an affidavit stating the dates of birth of his three sons.
He obtained this information from school records.
The affidavit incorrectly stated one son's date of birth as June 9, 1954, instead of the actual date, December 12, 1951.
The appellant claimed this was a bona fide mistake.
The High Court rejected this plea and ordered his prosecution for making a false statement under sections 199 and 200 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.).
law: To establish an offense under Section 199 of the I.P.C., the false statement must be 'touching any point material to the object for which the declaration is made'.
To establish an offense under Section 200 of the I.P.C., the declaration must be used or attempted to be used 'corruptly'.
application: The Supreme Court found that the incorrect date of birth was not material to the legal issues in the High Court appeal; it did not affect the decision on whether to implead the son or the maintainability of the suit.
The Court noted that it was not shown how the declaration was used 'corruptly'.
Crucially, the Court observed that the appellant 'stood to gain no advantage' by providing the wrong date.
The Court also considered that the appellant had obtained the incorrect information from school records, which supported his claim of a mistake rather than a deliberate falsehood.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in directing the prosecution because the essential legal requirements for an offense under sections 199 and 200 I.P.C. were not met. The false statement was not material to the case, and there was no evidence that it was used corruptly or that the appellant gained any advantage from it. Therefore, the appeal was allowed and the complaint was quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the false statement in the affidavit regarding the son's date of birth was material to the object for which the declaration was made, as required for an offence under Section 199 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The false statement was not material because the appellant stood to gain no advantage by giving a wrong date of birth for his son.
The purpose of the affidavit was to add the sons as parties, and for this purpose, the exact date of birth was not a material fact.
respondent_arguments: The statement was material because it was deliberately given in a sworn affidavit as required by the court.
The fact that the appellant thought the false date could be supported by a school certificate indicates he treated it as a material statement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant used the declaration containing the false statement 'corruptly', as required for an offence under Section 200 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The declaration was not used 'corruptly' as there was no corrupt motive.
The fact that the appellant stood to gain no advantage from the incorrect statement negates any corrupt intent.
respondent_arguments: The declaration was used corruptly because it contained a statement that was deliberately and knowingly false, which constitutes an attempt to mislead the court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the prosecution of the appellant, considering he stood to gain no advantage from the incorrect statement and had obtained the information from school records.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution was unjustified because the appellant stood to gain no advantage from the incorrect statement.
The error was a result of a bona fide mistake, as the appellant, having a large family, did not remember the exact date and obtained the information from school records.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution was justified because the High Court rejected the plea of a bona fide mistake.
The High Court found that the false date was given deliberately, with the intention of supporting it with a school certificate, which is a serious act that warrants prosecution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To establish an offense under Section 199 of the Indian Penal Code, it must be proven that a false statement is material to the object for which the declaration is made. For an offense under Section 200, it is a necessary ingredient that the declaration was used or attempted to be used corruptly.
obiter: It is not necessary to consider whether the judgment directing the filing of a complaint was in contravention of s. 479A(6), Cr. P.C.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the prosecution of the appellant was unjustified because the essential ingredients for offences under Sections 199 and 200 of the Indian Penal Code were not satisfied. The incorrect statement about the son's date of birth was not material to the object of the affidavit, which was simply to implead the son as a party. Furthermore, the declaration was not used 'corruptly' as the appellant stood to gain no advantage from the error and had obtained the incorrect information from school records, negating any corrupt intent.
legal_tests_applied: For an offence under Section 199 of the Indian Penal Code, it must be proved that the false statement is 'touching any point material to the object for which the declaration is made'.
For an offence under Section 200 of the Indian Penal Code, one of the ingredients is that the declaration should be used or attempted to be used corruptly.
policy_considerations: The court determined that a criminal complaint should not have been directed where the false statement was not material to the judicial proceedings, the appellant stood to gain no advantage from the error, and the information was obtained from an external source (school records), suggesting a lack of corrupt motive rather than a deliberate attempt to mislead the court for gain.
